claim: PostgreSQL has built-in declarative partitioning by range, list and hash.
quotes: PostgreSQL offers built-in support for the following forms of partitioning:
Range Partitioning: The table is partitioned into "ranges" defined by a key column or set of columns, with no overlap between the ranges of values assigned to different partitions.
List Partitioning: The table is partitioned by explicitly listing which key value(s) appear in each partition.
Hash Partitioning: The table is partitioned by specifying a modulus and a remainder for each partition.

claim: Declarative partitioning arrived in PostgreSQL 10 with range and list only.
quotes: Declarative table partitioning
Add table partitioning syntax that automatically creates partition constraints and handles routing of tuple insertions and updates (Amit Langote)
The syntax supports range and list partitioning.

claim: Hash partitioning and execution-time partition pruning were added in PostgreSQL 11.
quotes: Allow the creation of partitions based on hashing a key column (Amul Sul)
Allow partition elimination during query execution (David Rowley, Beena Emerson)
Previously, partition elimination only happened at planning time, meaning many joins and prepared queries could not use partition elimination.

claim: A unique or primary key on a partitioned table must include all partition key columns, because each partition's index only enforces uniqueness locally.
quotes: To create a unique or primary key constraint on a partitioned table, the partition keys must not include any expressions or function calls and the constraint's columns must include all of the partition key columns. This limitation exists because the individual indexes making up the constraint can only directly enforce uniqueness within their own partitions; therefore, the partition structure itself must guarantee that there are not duplicates in different partitions.

claim: DETACH PARTITION CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 14) takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the parent instead of ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
quotes: ALTER TABLE measurement DETACH PARTITION measurement_y2006m02 CONCURRENTLY;

the first form of the command requires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the parent table. Adding the CONCURRENTLY qualifier as in the second form allows the detach operation to require only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock on the parent table.
Allow partitions to be detached in a non-blocking manner (Álvaro Herrera)
The syntax is ALTER TABLE ... DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY, and FINALIZE.

claim: A partitioned table can have a DEFAULT partition, which is scanned when a new partition is attached unless a CHECK constraint excludes the new range.
quotes: Similarly, if the partitioned table has a DEFAULT partition, it is recommended to create a CHECK constraint which excludes the to-be-attached partition's constraint. If this is not done, the DEFAULT partition will be scanned to verify that it contains no records which should be located in the partition being attached.

claim: Partition pruning happens at plan time and also at execution time, and is controlled by enable_partition_pruning (default on).
quotes: Partition pruning can be performed not only during the planning of a given query, but also during its execution.
Partition pruning may also be performed here to remove partitions using values which are only known during actual query execution.
Partition pruning can be disabled using the enable_partition_pruning setting.

Enables or disables the query planner's ability to eliminate a partitioned table's partitions from query plans. This also controls the planner's ability to generate query plans which allow the query executor to remove (ignore) partitions during query execution.

claim: The planner copes with up to a few thousand partitions if most are pruned; unpruned partitions raise planning time and per-session memory.
quotes: The query planner is generally able to handle partition hierarchies with up to a few thousand partitions fairly well, provided that typical queries allow the query planner to prune all but a small number of partitions. Planning times become longer and memory consumption becomes higher when more partitions remain after the planner performs partition pruning.
each partition requires its metadata to be loaded into the local memory of each session that touches it.

claim: Partitionwise join and partitionwise aggregate exist since PostgreSQL 11 but are off by default because they raise planning cost and memory.
quotes: enable_partitionwise_join ... Default: off
enable_partitionwise_aggregate ... Default: off
Partitionwise join currently applies only when the join conditions include all the partition keys, which must be of the same data type and have one-to-one matching sets of child partitions.
Query planning also becomes significantly more expensive in terms of memory and CPU.
This feature is disabled by default but can be enabled by changing enable_partitionwise_join.

claim: Hot standby lets clients run read-only queries on a standby, whose data is eventually consistent with the primary.
quotes: Hot standby is the term used to describe the ability to connect to the server and run read-only queries while the server is in archive recovery or standby mode.

The data on the standby takes some time to arrive from the primary server so there will be a measurable delay between primary and standby. Running the same query nearly simultaneously on both primary and standby might therefore return differing results. We say that data on the standby is eventually consistent with the primary. Once the commit record for a transaction is replayed on the standby, the changes made by that transaction will be visible to any new snapshots taken on the standby.

claim: max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30 s) is how long replay waits before cancelling standby queries that conflict with incoming WAL.
quotes: When hot standby is active, this parameter determines how long the standby server should wait before canceling standby queries that conflict with about-to-be-applied WAL entries
The default is 30 seconds. A value of -1 allows the standby to wait forever for conflicting queries to complete.
Conflicting queries will be canceled once it has taken longer than the relevant delay setting to apply any newly-received WAL data.

claim: hot_standby_feedback (default off) avoids cleanup conflicts by holding back VACUUM on the primary, at the cost of possible bloat there.
quotes: This parameter can be used to eliminate query cancels caused by cleanup records, but can cause database bloat on the primary for some workloads.
The default value is off.

prevents VACUUM from removing recently-dead rows and so cleanup conflicts do not occur. If you do this, you should note that this will delay cleanup of dead rows on the primary, which may result in undesirable table bloat.

claim: pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() on a standby returns the last WAL position replayed, the basis for read-your-writes checks.
quotes: Returns the last write-ahead log location that has been replayed during recovery. If recovery is still in progress this will increase monotonically.

claim: pg_stat_replication on the primary reports write_lag, flush_lag and replay_lag per standby.
quotes: write_lag: Time elapsed between flushing recent WAL locally and receiving notification that this standby server has written it (but not yet flushed it or applied it).
flush_lag: Time elapsed between flushing recent WAL locally and receiving notification that this standby server has written and flushed it (but not yet applied it).

replay_lag: Time elapsed between flushing recent WAL locally and receiving notification that this standby server has written, flushed and applied it. This can be used to gauge the delay that synchronous_commit level remote_apply incurred while committing if this server was configured as a synchronous standby.

claim: WAIT FOR LSN is new in PostgreSQL 19 (in beta 4 as of 2026-09-24, not yet released); PostgreSQL 18 has no such command or function.
quotes: A new WAIT command that waits until a standby has replayed changes up to a chosen point, thereby supporting "read-your-writes" query patterns on standbys.
Add WAIT command to allow standbys to wait for LSN values to be written, flushed, or replayed (Kartyshov Ivan, Alexander Korotkov, Xuneng Zhou)
WAIT FOR LSN 'lsn' [ WITH ( option [, ...] ) ] where option can be: MODE 'mode' TIMEOUT 'timeout' NO_THROW and mode can be: standby_replay | standby_write | standby_flush | primary_flush
The possible return values are success, timeout, and not in recovery.
September 24, 2026: PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4 Released!
version_or_date: PostgreSQL 19 Beta 4; release notes 'AS OF 2026-09-14'. PG 18 functions-admin page checked: no WAIT/pg_wal_replay_wait; whether a pg_wal_replay_wait procedure was committed then reverted during the 18 cycle is unconfirmed

claim: libpq's target_session_attrs picks a host from a multi-host list by role: any, read-write, read-only, primary, standby or prefer-standby.
quotes: It's typically used in combination with multiple host names to select the first acceptable alternative among several hosts. There are six modes:
read-write: session must accept read-write transactions by default (that is, the server must not be in hot standby mode and the default_transaction_read_only parameter must be off)
prefer-standby: first try to find a standby server, but if none of the listed hosts is a standby server, try again in any mode

claim: load_balance_hosts=random (PostgreSQL 16) shuffles hosts per connection and can be combined with target_session_attrs to spread connections over standbys only.
quotes: This parameter can be used in combination with target_session_attrs to, for example, load balance over standby servers only. Once successfully connected, subsequent queries on the returned connection will all be sent to the same server.
random: Hosts and addresses are tried in random order.
Allow multiple libpq-specified hosts to be randomly selected (Jelte Fennema)
This is enabled with load_balance_hosts=random and can be used for load balancing.

claim: Jepsen found that RDS for PostgreSQL multi-AZ clusters violate Snapshot Isolation, allowing Long Fork even when healthy.
quotes: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL multi-AZ clusters violate Snapshot Isolation, the strongest consistency model supported across all endpoints. Healthy clusters occasionally allow Long Fork and other G-nonadjacent cycles.

claim: Long Fork means two transactions each update a different row and two readers see them in opposite orders, so neither fork observes the other.
quotes: Each fork updates a different row, but neither fork observes the other's effects
T1 appended 9 to row 89, resulting in the list [4 9], which T2 observed. T3 appended 11 to row 90
T2 observed T1's append to row 89, it failed to observe T3's append to row 90.

claim: The root cause is that the primary makes commits visible in ProcArray lock order while replicas make them visible in WAL order, and the two orders can differ.
quotes: the order in which a PostgreSQL primary makes transactions visible is determined by an in-memory lock. Secondaries, however, make transactions visible based on their order in the Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The lock order and WAL order can be different.
a transaction makes itself durable by recording its status in the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and then asynchronously removes itself from the ProcArray.

claim: AWS states the behaviour is not RDS-specific and reproduces on self-managed PostgreSQL with read replicas.
quotes: This behavior is not specific to Amazon RDS. It can be reproduced on self-managed PostgreSQL deployments.

claim: The proposed fix is Commit Sequence Numbers (CSNs), a multi-patch community effort; as of the PostgreSQL 19 beta release notes it has not shipped.
quotes: Commit Sequence Numbers (CSNs)
rather involved and spans multiple patches
Jepsen encourages both AWS and PostgreSQL to document this issue while they work to fix it.
version_or_date: AWS blog 2025-05-02; PG 19 release notes (beta, as of 2026-09-14) checked: no mention of CSN or standby visibility order

claim: No later Jepsen re-test or confirmed community fix for Long Fork on replicas was found; the pgsql-hackers CSN thread status could not be fetched.
Citus 14.0 (released 2026-02-17) added PostgreSQL 18 support; 14.2.0 is the newest 14.x release seen on GitHub.
quotes: Citus 14.0 brings PostgreSQL 18.1 support, and more!
version_or_date: v14.0.0 2026-02-17; v14.2.0 released 'August 6' (year not shown on page; the fetch tool reported 2024, which cannot be right for a release after 14.0, so 2026 is inferred). docs.citusdata.com/en/latest still labelled 13.0.1

claim: A Citus distributed table is hash-sharded on a distribution column into shards on worker nodes, using create_distributed_table.
quotes: These appear to be normal tables to SQL statements, but are horizontally partitioned across worker nodes.
algorithmic sharding to assign rows to shards. This means the assignment is made deterministically [dash] in our case based on the value of a particular table column called the distribution column.
takes in a table name, the distribution column and an optional distribution method.
version_or_date: Citus docs (labelled 13.0.1); one quote's source dash shown as [dash]

claim: The default shard count for a hash-distributed table is 32 (citus.shard_count), settable per table from 1 to 64000.
quotes: Sets the shard count for hash-partitioned tables and defaults to 32.
the number of shards to create for the new distributed table

claim: A reference table is a single shard replicated to every worker, and writes to it use two-phase commit.
quotes: A reference table is a type of distributed table whose entire contents are concentrated into a single shard which is replicated on every worker.
when interacting with a reference table we automatically perform two-phase commits (2PC) on transactions
Writes to a reference table are performed using 2PC and use aggressive locking to avoid diverging.
version_or_date: Citus docs; source README on main

claim: Tables distributed on the same column can be co-located (colocate_with), and joins on the distribution keys are pushed down to the shards.
quotes: Tables are co-located in groups. To manually control a table's co-location group assignment use the optional colocate_with parameter of create_distributed_table.

Citus knows that the entire query can be answered using the set of co-located shards that contain the data for that particular tenant, and the PostgreSQL node can answer the query in a single step, which enables full SQL support.

Query Pushdown can route a query to multiple shards across multiple nodes. Instead of verifying that all tables have the same filters, as in Router Planning, Query Pushdown ascertains that all tables are joined on their distribution keys.
version_or_date: Citus docs; source README on main

claim: Schema-based sharding (since Citus 12.0) makes each schema a logical shard; citus.enable_schema_based_sharding distributes new schemas automatically.
quotes: Available since Citus 12.0, schema-based sharding is the shared database, separate schema model, the schema becomes the logical shard within the database.
With the parameter set to ON all created schemas will be distributed by default.

claim: The shard rebalancer moves shards with logical replication, non-blocking for reads and writes since Citus 11.0; citus_rebalance_start replaces the deprecated rebalance_table_shards.
quotes: Citus's shard rebalancing uses PostgreSQL logical replication to move data from the old shard (called the 'publisher' in replication terms) to the new (the 'subscriber.')
Starting in version 11.0, Citus Community edition now supports non-blocking reads and writes during rebalancing.
version_or_date: Citus 11.0+; rebalance_table_shards deprecated as of 11.2 (per api_udf page, paraphrased by fetch tool)

claim: Transactions that write to several nodes commit with PostgreSQL's two-phase commit, with a maintenance daemon recovering failed prepared transactions.
quotes: For transactions that involve multiple nodes, Citus uses two-phase commit for atomicity and implements distributed deadlock detection.

For transactions that write to multiple nodes, Citus uses the built-in two-phase commit (2PC) machinery in PostgreSQL. In the pre-commit callback, a "prepare transaction" command is sent over all connections to worker nodes with open transaction blocks, then a commit record is stored on the coordinator.
The maintenance daemon takes care of recovering failed 2PC transactions by comparing the commit records on the coordinator to the list of pending prepared transactions on the worker.
version_or_date: Citus source README on main. Note: an older docs page (reference_dml) still says multi-shard updates default to one-phase commit; the GUC page says citus.multi_shard_commit_protocol defaults to 2pc

claim: Citus multi-node transactions are atomic but do not provide distributed snapshot isolation, because prepared transactions commit at different times on different nodes.
quotes: Multi-node transactions provide atomicity, consistency, and durability guarantees. Since the prepared transactions commit at different times, they do not provide distributed snapshot isolation guarantees.
If Citus provided serializability, there could only be 2 outcomes (a happens first or b happens first). However, it can have at least 4 outcomes

claim: Microsoft acquired Citus Data in January 2019.
quotes: I am thrilled to announce that we have acquired Citus Data, a leader in the PostgreSQL community.

claim: Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL is on a retirement path; Microsoft now points PostgreSQL scale-out users to elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, a managed Citus.
quotes: Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL is on a retirement path and no longer recommended for new projects.

For PostgreSQL workloads, use the Elastic Clusters feature of Azure Database For PostgreSQL to take advantage of horizontal scale-out and distributed PostgreSQL features within the open source Citus extension.
Elastic clusters on the Azure Database for PostgreSQL service are a managed offering of the open-source Citus extension to PostgreSQL that enables horizontal sharding of PostgreSQL.
Rebalancing is an online operation and doesn't block running workloads.
version_or_date: Cosmos page updated 2026-04-27; elastic clusters page ms.date 2026-07-08 (elastic clusters GA date not stated on page: unconfirmed)

claim: The current stable Vitess documentation is v24.0, with v25.0 in development.
quotes: # Release of Vitess v24.0.0

claim: A Vitess keyspace is a logical database that maps to many MySQL databases when sharded.
quotes: A keyspace is a logical database. If you're using sharding, a keyspace maps to multiple MySQL databases; if you're not using sharding, a keyspace maps directly to a MySQL database name.

claim: A shard is a subset of a keyspace with one MySQL primary and replicas; shard names are hex key ranges such as -80 and 80-.
quotes: A shard is a subset of a keyspace. A keyspace will always contain one or more shards. A shard typically contains one MySQL primary and potentially many MySQL replicas.
The replicas can serve read-only traffic (with eventual consistency guarantees), execute long-running data analysis queries, or perform administrative tasks (backup, restore, diff, etc.).

claim: The VSchema describes how data is laid out across keyspaces and shards and drives query routing and resharding.
quotes: A VSchema allows you to describe how data is organized within keyspaces and shards. This information is used for routing queries, and also during resharding operations.

claim: A vindex maps a column value to a keyspace ID; every sharded table needs a unique primary vindex (often hash), and lookup vindexes store value-to-keyspace-ID mappings in backing tables.
quotes: A Vindex provides a way to map a column value to a Keyspace ID.
Every sharded table must have one defined. A Primary Vindex must be unique: given an input value, it must produce a single keyspace ID.
create and store associations between column values and keyspace IDs, allowing them to be recalled later.
return a single or a limited set of keyspace IDs which will allow VTGate to only target shards where the relevant data is present.
version_or_date: v24.0 (hash vindex described on page as a DES null-key hash; quote via fetch summary)

claim: VTGate is the stateless proxy that routes queries to vttablets; a tablet is a mysqld plus a vttablet process.
quotes: VTGate is a lightweight proxy server that routes traffic to the correct VTTablet servers and returns consolidated results back to the client.
A tablet is a combination of a mysqld process and a corresponding vttablet process, usually running on the same machine.

claim: Resharding is a Reshard workflow built on VReplication: copy and stream changes to target shards, verify with VDiff, SwitchTraffic, then complete.
quotes: create and manage workflows to horizontally shard an existing keyspace
switches traffic forward for the tablet-types specified
establishes replication from a source keyspace/shard to a target keyspace/shard.

claim: Vitess transaction_mode is SINGLE, MULTI (best effort, no atomicity) or TWOPC (atomic commit across shards, without cross-shard isolation).
quotes: Single | Transactions limited to one shard | Simple CRUD operations | Full ACID
Multi | Can span multiple shards with best-effort commits | Bulk updates where partial success is acceptable | No atomicity
TwoPC | Atomic commits across multiple shards | Financial transactions, inventory updates | Atomic commits
While TwoPC guarantees atomicity (all-or-nothing commits), it does not provide isolation in the traditional ACID sense.
Applications might observe fractured reads in a cross-shard query i.e. a query might see partial commits while a TwoPC transaction commit is in progress.
TwoPC transactions will roll back if semi-sync is not enabled

claim: Atomic distributed transactions (TWOPC) were introduced as experimental in Vitess v21; no release note declaring them GA was found in v22 to v24, and the v24 docs no longer call them experimental.
quotes: We have introduced atomic distributed transactions as an experimental feature.
version_or_date: v21.0.0 experimental; GA status in v22+ unconfirmed

claim: PlanetScale announced PlanetScale for Postgres on 2025-07-01 and later marked it Generally Available; Vitess itself is built around MySQL.
quotes: PlanetScale for Postgres is now Generally Available
Vitess' achievements are enabled by leveraging MySQL's strengths and engineering around its weaknesses
version_or_date: announced 2025-07-01; exact GA date not shown in fetched text (unconfirmed)

claim: Neki, PlanetScale's sharded Postgres (not a Vitess fork), is now available, with cross-shard transactions still marked coming soon.
quotes: Neki is sharded Postgres by PlanetScale. Every shard is real Postgres. Neki adds the router, sidecars, and control plane to scale it past a single machine, to hundreds of millions of QPS and petabytes of data, without downtime.
Neki, sharded Postgres, is now available.
Neki is not a fork of Vitess.
Cross-shard transactions
Coming soon
version_or_date: neki.dev as of 2026-10-05 (blog posts Sep-Oct 2026); exact launch date unconfirmed

claim: Multigres is Supabase's Vitess adaptation for Postgres, led by Vitess co-creator Sugu Sougoumarane since June 2025, and is still in early development.
quotes: Today we're welcoming Sugu, the co-creator of Vitess, to the Supabase team. He is joining Supabase to build Multigres: Vitess for Postgres.
Multigres is a Vitess adaptation for Postgres. The project is currently in the early stages of development.
A horizontally scalable architecture for PostgreSQL supporting multi-tenant, highly available, and globally distributed deployments, while staying true to standard Postgres.
version_or_date: announced 2025-06-10; README on main as of 2026-10-05; latest blog post 2026-09-08

claim: CockroachDB splits its sorted key space into ranges, by default at most 512 MiB (min 128 MiB), and splits a range automatically when it grows past that.
quotes: contiguous chunks of the key-space
range_max_bytes: Default: 536870912 (512 MiB)
range_min_bytes: Default: 134217728 (128 MiB)
version_or_date: stable docs (site lists versions up to v26.4)

claim: Each range is a Raft group, replicated 3 ways by default (5 for system ranges).
quotes: organizes all nodes that contain a replica of a range into a group--unsurprisingly called a Raft group.
num_replicas: Default: 3
3 is the smallest number that can achieve quorum (i.e., 2 out of 3)

claim: One replica per range holds the lease and is the only one that serves strongly consistent reads or proposes writes; since v25.2 leases are leader leases tied to Raft leadership.
quotes: is the only node that can serve reads or propose writes to the Raft group leader.
leaseholders bypass Raft
version_or_date: stable docs (v26.x); leader leases v25.2+ (paraphrased by fetch tool)

claim: Follower reads serve slightly stale data from the nearest replica using AS OF SYSTEM TIME follower_read_timestamp(), which is about 4.8 s in the past.
quotes: A follower read is performed on the nearest replica relative to the SQL gateway
SELECT ... FROM ... AS OF SYSTEM TIME follower_read_timestamp();

Can tolerate reading older data (at least 4.2 seconds in the past), to reduce the chance that the historical query timestamp is not quite old enough to prevent blocking on a conflicting write and thus being able to be served by a local replica.
It is otherwise hardcoded as -4.8s from the statement time, which may not result in reading from the nearest replica.
version_or_date: stable docs (v26.x). Note: the -4.8s figure is in the function reference, in the text describing the fallback when no enterprise licence is present

claim: Multi-region tables are REGIONAL BY TABLE (fast in one home region), REGIONAL BY ROW (each row has its own home region) or GLOBAL (fast reads everywhere, slower writes).
quotes: In a regional table, access to the table will be fast in the table's home region and slower in other regions.
In a regional by row table, each row is optimized for access from a specific home region.
A global table is optimized for low-latency reads from every region in the database.
writes will incur higher latencies from any given region, since writes have to be replicated across every region.

claim: Survival goals are ZONE (default) or REGION; surviving a region needs at least 3 regions and adds at least one inter-region round trip to writes.
quotes: the database will remain fully available for reads and writes, even if a zone becomes unavailable
the database will remain fully available for reads and writes, even if an entire region becomes unavailable.
The zone failure survival goal is the default.
To survive region failures, you must add at least 3 database regions.
write latency will be increased by at least as much as the round-trip time to the nearest region. Read performance will be unaffected.

claim: CockroachDB runs transactions at SERIALIZABLE by default and also offers READ COMMITTED.
quotes: By default, CockroachDB executes all transactions at the strongest ANSI transaction isolation level: SERIALIZABLE
CockroachDB offers two transaction isolation levels: SERIALIZABLE and READ COMMITTED.

claim: From v24.3 CockroachDB has Enterprise, Enterprise Free (under 10M USD revenue, telemetry required) and 30-day Trial licences.
quotes: all versions of CockroachDB starting from the release date of 24.3.0 onward
Same functionality as Enterprise, but free of charge for businesses with less than $10M in annual revenue.
30 day self-service trial license
There is a 7 day grace period for Enterprise Free and Enterprise Trial clusters to (re)start sending telemetry.

claim: An unlicensed multi-node cluster is throttled to 5 concurrent open transactions 7 days after initialisation; single-node clusters and cockroach demo need no licence, so a short local 3-node demo is fine but the docs do not explicitly exempt multi-node demos.
quotes: If no valid license key is ever entered, the cluster will be throttled 7 days after cluster initialization.
When a cluster is being throttled, the number of concurrent open SQL transactions is limited to 5.
No license key is required for developers running single-node clusters using the following cockroach commands: cockroach start-single-node, cockroach demo.
Single-node clusters are not throttled.

claim: YugabyteDB splits tables into tablets; in YSQL the first primary key column is hash-sharded by default unless ASC/DESC range sharding is declared.
quotes: for every key, there is exactly one tablet that owns it
By default, only the first column is treated as the hash-partition column. But this behavior can be modified by explicit use of the HASH annotation.
If the primary key specification is PRIMARY KEY(a, b), then column a is used to hash partition the table, and rows that share the same value for a are stored in ascending order of their value for b.

claim: Each YugabyteDB tablet is replicated by its own Raft group of tablet peers with an elected leader.
quotes: Each tablet comprises of a set of tablet peers, each of which stores one copy of the data belonging to the tablet.
As soon as a tablet initiates, it elects one of the tablet peers as the tablet leader using the Raft protocol.
The replication of data between the tablet peers is strongly consistent

claim: TiKV stores data in Regions ([StartKey, EndKey) ranges), each a Raft group; the default split size is 256 MiB since v8.4.0 (was 96 MiB).
quotes: Each Region can be described by [StartKey, EndKey), a left-closed and right-open interval.
the default size limit for each Region is 256 MiB and the size can be configured.
multiple Replicas of a Region are stored on different nodes to form a Raft Group, which is kept consistent through the Raft algorithm.
Default value: "256MiB". Prior to v8.4.0, it was "96MiB".
version_or_date: TiDB stable docs; default changed in v8.4.0

claim: The Placement Driver (PD) tracks which Region holds each key and spreads Regions evenly across TiKV nodes.
quotes: as evenly as possible across all nodes in the cluster
the distribution of Regions on the node, that is, the exact Region of a Key and the node of that Region placed through any Key.

claim: Spanner divides each table into splits (contiguous key ranges) that it adds and removes by size and load, so monotonically increasing keys create a write hotspot.
quotes: A split holds a range of contiguous rows. The start and end keys of this range are called 'split boundaries'.
Spanner automatically adds and removes split boundaries based on size and load, which changes the number of splits in the database.

if you insert records with a monotonically increasing integer as the key, you'll always insert at the end of your key space. This is undesirable because Spanner divides data among servers by key ranges, which means your inserts will be directed at a single server, creating a hotspot.

claim: In the 2012 Spanner paper, each spanserver runs one Paxos state machine per tablet.
quotes: each spanserver is responsible for between 100 and 1000 instances of a data structure called a tablet.
To support replication, each spanserver implements a single Paxos state machine on top of each tablet.

claim: TrueTime returns an interval; its uncertainty epsilon is a sawtooth of about 1 to 7 ms (about 4 ms most of the time), and commit wait makes a write wait about 2 times epsilon before it becomes visible.
quotes: The TT.now() method returns a TTinterval that is guaranteed to contain the absolute time during which TT.now() was invoked.
In our production environment, ε is typically a sawtooth function of time, varying from about 1 to 7 ms over each poll interval. ε̄ is therefore 4 ms most of the time.

The daemon's poll interval is currently 30 seconds, and the current applied drift rate is set at 200 microseconds/second, which together account for the sawtooth bounds from 0 to 6 ms. The remaining 1 ms comes from the communication delay to the time masters.
The coordinator leader ensures that clients cannot see any data committed by Ti until TT.after(si) is true.
the expected wait is at least 2 ∗ ε̄. This wait is typically overlapped with Paxos communication.
version_or_date: Corbett et al., OSDI 2012 (Greek symbols lost in PDF text extraction and restored from the paper's notation)

claim: Amazon Aurora DSQL became generally available on 2025-05-27 as a serverless distributed SQL database with active-active, multi-Region strong consistency.
quotes: Today, AWS announces the general availability of Amazon Aurora DSQL, the fastest serverless, distributed SQL database with active-active high availability and multi-Region strong consistency.
The active-active highly available architecture provides 99.99% single-Region and 99.999% multi-Region availability.
Both endpoints of a peered cluster present a single logical database. They are available for concurrent read and write operations, and provide strong data consistency.

claim: Aurora DSQL multi-Region clusters must stay within one continent's Region set; cross-continent clusters are not supported.
quotes: You must create multi-Region clusters within a single Region set.
Aurora DSQL currently doesn't support cross-continent multi-Region clusters.

claim: Aurora DSQL uses optimistic concurrency control: no locks, conflicts detected at commit and returned as SQLSTATE 40001 (OC000), so clients must retry.
quotes: Aurora DSQL uses optimistic concurrency control (OCC), which works differently from traditional lock-based systems. Instead of using locks, OCC evaluates conflicts at commit time.
When Aurora DSQL detects a conflict, it returns a PostgreSQL serialization failure with SQLSTATE code 40001.
ERROR: change conflicts with another transaction (OC000) (SQLSTATE 40001)
Two transactions attempted to modify the same row. The transaction with the earliest commit time succeeds

claim: An Aurora DSQL transaction may modify at most 3,000 rows and 10 MiB and last at most 5 minutes; connections last at most 60 minutes.
quotes: Maximum size of all data modified in a write transaction | 10 MiB
Maximum number of table rows that can be mutated in a transaction block | 3,000 rows per transaction.
Maximum transaction time | 5 minutes
Maximum connection duration | 60 minutes

claim: Aurora DSQL is PostgreSQL 16 compatible but fixed at Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation), one database per cluster, with no temporary tables, triggers, PL/pgSQL or TRUNCATE, and one DDL statement per transaction; foreign keys are now supported.
quotes: Aurora DSQL is currently compatible with PostgreSQL version 16
The transaction isolation level is fixed at PostgreSQL Repeatable Read.
DDL and DML operations require separate transactions
A transaction can include only 1 DDL statement
Aurora DSQL supports SQL-based functions but not procedural languages like PL/pgSQL.
Use DELETE FROM table_name instead of TRUNCATE.
Aurora DSQL supports the NO ACTION, RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL, and SET DEFAULT referential actions.
version_or_date: AWS docs accessed 2026-10-05; when foreign key support was added is unconfirmed

claim: Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database became generally available on 2024-10-31.
quotes: Today, AWS announces the general availability of Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database, which helps you scale your Amazon Aurora cluster to millions of write transactions per second and manage petabytes of data while maintaining the simplicity of operating inside a single database.

claim: Limitless runs a DB shard group of routers and shards, with hash-sharded tables, collocated tables, reference tables copied to every shard, and standard tables on one shard.
quotes: Nodes are either routers or shards.
DB shard group: A container for Limitless Database nodes (shards and routers).
Sharding is hash-based, not range- or list-based.
Collocated tables: Two sharded tables that share the same shard key and are explicitly declared as collocated. All data for the same shard key value is sent to the same shard.
Reference table: A table with its data copied in full on every shard.
All standard tables are stored on the same shard selected by the system

claim: PgDog is an open-source Rust Postgres proxy that pools connections, load balances replicas, and shards: it parses queries to extract the sharding key, routes them, and merges cross-shard results in memory.
quotes: PgDog is an open source proxy for scaling PostgreSQL. It supports connection pooling, load balancing queries and sharding entire databases.
By using the PostgreSQL parser, PgDog extracts sharding keys and determines the best routing strategy for each query.
For cross-shard queries, PgDog assembles and transforms results in memory, sending all rows to the client as if they are coming from a single database.
The PARTITION BY HASH algorithm is used by default when configuring sharded tables
To make sure cross-shard writes are atomic, PgDog supports Postgres' two-phase transactions.

claim: PgDog says it is used in production at scale, with some sharding features still experimental, and can reshard live using logical replication.
quotes: PgDog is used in production and at scale. Most features are stable, while some are experimental.
New sharding features are added almost weekly.
PgDog understands the PostgreSQL logical replication protocol and can orchestrate data splits between databases, in the background and without downtime.
